mappings.note: Mass of one molecule scaled by Avogadro's number to give a molecular mass of 28 u. The destination is molecular mass, which LO-41 names, but the route is the mole. POOR FIT on the route: no legal code names Avogadro's number or the mole.

Weighted average of the 35 u and 37 u chlorine isotopes in a 3:1 ratio. POOR FIT: LO-41's calculation list is ion charge, valency from the atomic number, and molecular and formula unit mass - an isotopic average atomic mass is none of these, and isotopes are not mentioned anywhere in the legal set. LO-41 is cited as the only calculation outcome available.
Formula unit masses of ZnO, Na2O and K2CO3 from given atomic masses. The cleanest LO-41 item in this part - no mole, no Avogadro, exactly the calculation the outcome enumerates.
Mass of a single carbon atom from the 12 g mole. The bridge from bulk mass to one particle, so LO-48's particle clause joins LO-41. POOR FIT: the mole is the whole mechanism and it is unmapped.

Masses of 1 mole of N atoms, 4 moles of Al and 10 moles of Na2SO3 - three mole-to-mass conversions differing only in the compound. Mapped together and honestly so: nothing in the frame distinguishes them. POOR FIT for the same reason as the rest of the mole block.

Equal masses of ethane and methane converted to a molecule count. The hardest particle-counting item in the chapter and the worst-served by the frame: it is pure Avogadro reasoning, and LO-41 plus LO-48 are cited only as the nearest available calculation and particle codes. POOR FIT.

(a) counts SO2 molecules in 44 g; (b) gets the mass of one oxygen atom from the 16 g mole. Molecules out and a single-atom mass out, both through molar mass. POOR FIT - the mole is absent from the legal set.

Atomic mass, gram atomic mass, then the atom count in 11.5 g of sodium. Part (a) is inside LO-41; parts (b) and (c) introduce gram atomic mass and Avogadro's number, neither of which any legal code names. POOR FIT.

Moles, molecules and atoms in 5.6 g of nitrogen - the three-step mole ladder, including the molecule-to-atom doubling. POOR FIT: the mole, the molar mass and Avogadro's number are all unmapped; LO-48's particle clause is the nearest thing to the counting idea.

Atoms in 0.5 mole of carbon - no mass appears anywhere in the item, only Avogadro's number halved. The single worst fit in the chapter: LO-48 leads because the answer is a count of particles, and LO-41 is cited only to keep it with the rest of the calculation family. POOR FIT.
Masses of 0.2 mole of oxygen atoms and 0.5 mole of water molecules. A twin of 115e539a with fractional moles; mapped identically because the frame supplies no distinction. POOR FIT on the mole.

(i) mass of 2 moles of CO2; (ii) mass of exactly one Avogadro number of CO2 molecules. Part (ii) is there to test that a mole IS 6.022 x 10^23 particles, which is precisely the idea the frame never names. POOR FIT.

Molar mass of sulphuric acid - numerically the molecular mass LO-41 names, differing only in units. The least damaged item in the mole block, and the reason LO-41 is the right nearest code for the rest of it.

Sunita's error is a molecular-mass error (S8 is 256 u, not 64 u), which is squarely LO-41; the follow-up asks for moles in 25.6 g, which is not. Cited on LO-41 for the graded half, with the mole half flagged as unmapped.

Counting atoms inside H2S and inside the phosphate ion is reading a formula's subscripts - the inverse of LO-42's writing clause - while the molecule/ion pairing is LO-39's species differentiation. Despite sitting in the mole block this item needs no mole at all.

Percentage composition worked straight from the measured masses of boron and oxygen in one sample. That is the law of constant proportions in use, LO-40 - unlike 4983fced, which reaches its percentages through the formula unit mass and therefore goes to LO-41.
Show that the sodium carbonate/acetic acid readings agree with the law. Verification against measured data, LO-39's fused conservation clause, and the long-answer form of the short item b7965e32.
Scale the 1:8 ratio to 3 g of hydrogen. Constant proportions applied, LO-40; the recall-only version of the same ratio (685ba20b, 4ebb12dd) sits on LO-48.

The case study asks which law is demonstrated and to state it (LO-48), then to solve the sealed-flask mass balance and say why sealing mattered (LO-39's verification clause). Not LO-49: nothing here appears to violate the law, the flask is sealed throughout.

A Dalton case study end to end - which law his postulate explains, what distinguishes gold from silver, how indivisible atoms still make compounds. All of it is LO-40's 'Explain the Dalton's atomic theory' clause.

Water from a river, a well and a synthesis all at 1:8, plus a decomposition calculation. LO-40 for the law applied across sources; C1.2 is added for the final part, which asks whether the law holds for salty water and so turns on what a mixture is.

Kanad and Democritus against Dalton: a history-of-ideas case study, which is C5.2's territory (science examined through a social-sciences lens), carrying the particulate concept (LO-48) and the question of what made Dalton's version scientific (LO-40). The only item in the chapter that genuinely needs all three.

Define and compute the molecular mass of H2SO4 (LO-41), then name the term used instead for an ionic compound (LO-39's molecular-mass/formula-unit-mass pair). The last part is what separates this from the plain H2SO4 computation f6e1e2c3.

What a symbol conveys, what H2O tells you, why IUPAC standardisation matters, and why the subscript appears in H2O but not NaCl. Every part is LO-42's 'scientific conventions, symbols' clause; the last part quietly requires knowing a formula unit is already in simplest ratio.

Why CuSO4 is not written Cu2(SO4)2, plus the copper(I) variant. The subscript-reduction rule and the polyatomic bracket, both LO-42. Its MCQ sibling 242c3f51 tests the same reduction on calcium carbonate.
